conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/name: Crusades and Holy Leagues against the Ottomans: Nicopolis, Varna, Lepanto and Vienna
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/religionR: Popes proclaimed crusades with indulgences and organised Holy Leagues, and both Christian and Ottoman sides framed the struggle as war for the faith (crusade against the ‘Turk’, ghaza and jihad for the Ottomans). But the wars were also, and often chiefly, contests between empires over territory, trade and dynastic power: Catholic France allied with the Ottomans from the 1530s, Venice repeatedly made separate peaces to protect its commerce, and Protestant princes bargained over aid against the Turks for religious concessions. Norman Housley argues that crusading remained a living ideology into the seventeenth century, while others treat late ‘crusades’ as primarily state wars with religious colouring.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/sides/0/n: Crusaders and Holy Leagues: papacy, Hungary, Poland, the Habsburgs, Venice, Spain and allies
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/sides/0/f: Latin Catholic, with Orthodox allies (Serbs, Wallachians, Byzantines) and, in the Habsburg wars, Protestant contingents
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/sides/0/l: Władysław III of Poland and Hungary
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/sides/1/f: Sunni Islam (with many Christian subjects and vassals)
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/summary: As the Ottomans advanced into the Balkans and central Europe, popes repeatedly called crusades and formed Holy Leagues against them. The crusades of Nicopolis (1396) and Varna (1444) ended in disaster, Constantinople fell in 1453, and Hungary was broken at Mohács in 1526. The Holy League’s naval victory at Lepanto in 1571 and the relief of Vienna in 1683, followed by the Holy League’s reconquest of Hungary, reversed the tide, ending with the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/story:
By the 1390s the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I had conquered Bulgaria and made Serbia a vassal after the battle of Kosovo (1389). King Sigismund of Hungary appealed to the West, and both rival popes of the Great Schism, Boniface IX in Rome and Benedict XIII in Avignon, proclaimed a crusade. A large army of Hungarians, French and Burgundian knights under John of Nevers, Germans, Hospitallers and Wallachians marched down the Danube in 1396 and besieged Nicopolis. On 25 September the Western knights charged ahead against Sigismund’s advice and were destroyed; Bayezid had several thousand prisoners executed in reprisal for the crusaders’ killing of captives at Rahova, and great nobles were held for ransom.

After the Council of Florence (1439) proclaimed union with the Greek Church, Pope Eugenius IV called a new crusade to save Constantinople. The Hungarian general John Hunyadi and King Władysław III of Poland and Hungary won victories in the ‘Long Campaign’ of 1443 and secured a truce in 1444, but, urged by the legate Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini, who argued that an oath to infidels did not bind, they broke it. At Varna on 10 November 1444 Murad II destroyed their army; the king and the cardinal were killed. On 29 May 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople after a seven-week siege; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, the city was sacked for a day and Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

Pope Callixtus III launched a crusade preached by the Franciscan John of Capistrano, whose peasant crusaders helped Hunyadi relieve the siege of Belgrade in July 1456; the pope’s order for church bells to be rung at noon to pray for the crusade became the noon Angelus bell. Pius II summoned princes to the Congress of Mantua in 1459 and took the cross himself, but died at Ancona in 1464 waiting for a fleet that never came. The Ottomans took Otranto in southern Italy in 1480, killing many inhabitants, including some 800 men later venerated as martyrs for refusing to convert. In 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, killing King Louis II, and in 1529 besieged Vienna. Francis I of France, ‘the Most Christian King’, allied with Suleiman against the Habsburgs, and Protestant princes in the Empire demanded religious concessions in return for votes of aid against the Turk.

In the Mediterranean the Hospitallers survived the Great Siege of Malta in 1565. When the Ottomans invaded Venetian Cyprus in 1570, Pope Pius V forged a Holy League with Spain and Venice, signed in May 1571. Famagusta fell in August 1571 and its commander Marco Antonio Bragadin was flayed alive after surrender. On 7 October 1571 the allied fleet under Don John of Austria destroyed the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in the Gulf of Patras, the largest galley battle in history; the Ottoman admiral Ali Pasha was killed and thousands of Christian galley slaves were freed. Pius V attributed the victory to the rosary and instituted a feast of Our Lady of Victory. The league soon dissolved: the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet, and Venice made a separate peace in 1573 ceding Cyprus.

In 1683 the grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged Vienna from mid-July. Pope Innocent XI had worked to bring Poland and the Emperor Leopold I together and financed the defence, and the Capuchin preacher Marco d’Aviano accompanied the relief army. On 12 September 1683 the army of the Empire and Poland under King Jan III Sobieski descended from the Kahlenberg and routed the Ottomans; Sobieski wrote to the pope, ‘We came, we saw, God conquered’. Innocent XI then formed a new Holy League in 1684 of the Empire, Poland and Venice, joined by Russia in 1686.

The League’s armies retook Buda in 1686, where the victors massacred many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, won the second battle of Mohács in 1687, and after a long war Eugene of Savoy crushed the Ottomans at Zenta in 1697. The Treaty of Karlowitz on 26 January 1699 gave Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs, Podolia to Poland and the Morea to Venice. It marked the first major Ottoman territorial retreat and is usually taken as the end of the Ottoman threat to central Europe and the last war that contemporaries widely described as a crusade.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/nameOfGod: Popes proclaimed crusade indulgences, levied crusade tithes and, from Callixtus III, ordered the faithful to pray at the noon bell for victory over the Turks; Lepanto was credited to the rosary and Vienna to Our Lady, giving rise to the feasts of Our Lady of the Rosary and the Holy Name of Mary (extended to the whole church by Innocent XI in 1683). Preachers such as John of Capistrano and Marco d’Aviano blessed the armies and carried the cross into battle. Protestant writers, including Luther, called for war against the Turk as a duty of the Christian ruler rather than as a crusade, while also interpreting the Turk as a scourge of God for Christian sins. On the Ottoman side, the sultans presented their conquests as ghaza and jihad, extending the abode of Islam.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/religious: Papal calls to defend Christendom and, after 1453, to recover Constantinople, backed by indulgences and crusade taxes.
The sense of a common Christian identity against the ‘Turk’, which preachers and printed pamphlets made a central theme of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century piety.
The fate of Orthodox and Catholic Christians under Ottoman rule, including the devshirme levy of Christian boys and enslavement in war.
Ottoman ideology of ghaza and holy war, which legitimised expansion into Christian lands.
Marian and Counter-Reformation devotion, which presented victories at Lepanto and Vienna as signs of divine favour for the Catholic Church.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/otherCaus: Ottoman imperial expansion into the Balkans, Hungary and the Mediterranean, and the strategic struggle with the Habsburgs for central Europe.
Venetian and Genoese commercial interests in the eastern Mediterranean, which drove both alliances and separate peaces.
Dynastic politics: the Habsburg–Valois rivalry led France to ally with the Ottomans, and Hungarian, Polish and Transylvanian princes balanced between the powers.
Control of Mediterranean sea lanes, corsair raids and the slave trade on both sides.
The internal politics of the Holy Roman Empire, where aid against the Turks was traded for Protestant concessions.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/triggers/: Bayezid I’s conquest of Bulgaria and pressure on Hungary, prompting the Nicopolis crusade of 1396.
The Ottoman threat to Constantinople after the Union of Florence (1439), leading to the Varna crusade of 1443–1444.
The Ottoman invasion of Venetian Cyprus in 1570, which produced the Holy League of 1571.
Kara Mustafa’s march on Vienna in 1683.

conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/casualtie: No total for three centuries of intermittent war can be given. Estimates exist for particular battles: at Lepanto modern historians (Capponi, Parker) suggest roughly 7,500–8,000 Holy League dead and some 20,000–30,000 Ottoman dead and captured, with perhaps 12,000–15,000 Christian galley slaves freed. Nicopolis, Varna and Mohács each cost many thousands of lives, and sieges such as Constantinople (1453), Belgrade (1456), Vienna (1683) and Buda (1686) killed soldiers and civilians in large numbers, but chronicle figures for these are unreliable.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effects/0: The Ottomans became the dominant power in south-eastern Europe for centuries, ruling large Orthodox Christian populations through the millet system.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effects/1: The fall of Constantinople ended the Byzantine Empire and moved the centre of Orthodox political hope to Moscow.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effects/2: Lepanto ended the aura of Ottoman naval invincibility, though not Ottoman power at sea.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effects/3: The relief of Vienna and the Treaty of Karlowitz began the long Ottoman retreat from central Europe and created the Habsburg Danubian monarchy.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effects/4: The Ottoman threat shaped the Reformation: Habsburg dependence on Protestant support against the Turk helped Protestantism survive in the Empire.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/effectsOn: Crusade preaching, crusade indulgences and ‘Turkish bells’ for prayer kept the crusading ideal alive in Catholic piety into the eighteenth century.
The feasts of Our Lady of the Rosary (from Lepanto) and of the Holy Name of Mary (from Vienna) entered the Catholic calendar.
Orthodox churches under Ottoman rule were organised under the patriarch of Constantinople, while the failure of Western aid deepened Orthodox suspicion of union with Rome after Florence.
Protestants and Catholics each interpreted the Turk apocalyptically and polemically, often as a judgement on the other side’s sins.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/legacy: The wars against the Ottomans fixed the image of the ‘Turk’ as the enemy of Christendom in European memory, from Lepanto paintings and Vienna’s celebrations to modern nationalist myths in the Balkans and appropriation by present-day anti-Muslim movements. Historians now emphasise the pragmatic diplomacy, trade and alliances that crossed religious lines throughout these centuries, alongside the genuine religious fervour of crusade preaching and of Ottoman ghaza.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/dissenter: In 1518 he wrote that to fight the Turks was to resist God’s punishment of Christian sins, a view condemned in the bull Exsurge Domine (1520); in On War against the Turk (1529) he rejected crusade under the banner of the Church, though he accepted the emperor’s duty to defend his subjects.

In the Complaint of Peace (1517) and his Consultation on War against the Turks (1530) he criticised crusade taxes and indulgences, warned that Christians fighting with the morals of Turks would themselves become Turks, and urged that Christ’s faith be spread by example rather than by the sword.

After the fall of Constantinople he wrote On the Peace of Faith (1453), imagining a heavenly council where representatives of the religions reach concord, and later sought to understand the Qur’an in his Sifting of the Qur’an.
The Spanish theologian proposed after 1453 that the Church seek peace and conferences with Muslims (‘per viam pacis et doctrinae’) instead of war, and prepared a new translation of the Qur’an.
conflicts/ottoman-holy-leagues/campaigns: Sigismund of Hungary, John of Nevers and the crusader army
The army gathered at Buda, crossed the Danube at the Iron Gates, took Vidin and Rahova, where prisoners were killed, and besieged Nicopolis until Bayezid’s relief army destroyed it on 25 September.
Władysław III, John Hunyadi and Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini

Having renounced the truce agreed at Szeged and Edirne, the crusaders crossed the Danube and marched east along the Bulgarian plain to the Black Sea coast, expecting a papal–Venetian fleet to block the Straits; Murad II crossed regardless and destroyed them at Varna.
The Holy League fleet to Lepanto
Don John of Austria with the Spanish, Venetian and papal galleys

The allied fleet of about 200 galleys and six galleasses assembled at Messina, sailed via Corfu and the Epirote coast, learned of the fall of Famagusta, and met the Ottoman fleet emerging from the Gulf of Lepanto on 7 October 1571.
Jan III Sobieski and the Polish army, joined by imperial and German forces

Sobieski left Kraków in August 1683, marched through Silesia and Moravia, joined the imperial army at Tulln and on 12 September descended from the Kahlenberg, where Marco d’Aviano had celebrated Mass, to break the siege.
